column1: # Optional keys (a?:1) — dropped from output when unresolved. Columns: name<TAB>mode<TAB>src<TAB>expect
# A PAIR IN LIST POSITION IS A SINGLE-KEY MAP ELEMENT: `[x:1]` is
# `[{x:1}]`, and `[x?:1]` is `[{x?:1}]` -- the `?` rides into the
# element, marking the KEY optional there, rather than changing what
# the pair is. This REVERSES the "not an element" rule these rows used
# to pin (issue #40): that rule was the least-bad answer to jsonic's
# raw slot write (a property for a text key, an INDEX for a numeric
# one), but it was itself a SILENT DROP -- `a:[x:1]` evaluated to
# `{"a":[]}`, the author's data gone at exit 0.
# THE BRACED TWIN IS THE INVARIANT: every row here answers
# byte-for-byte as its `[{...}]` spelling does, which is what makes
# the sugar a spelling rather than a semantics. The merge row is the
# old block's fear made a rule: two statements of one list meet
# ELEMENTWISE, so the single-key element merges into the map at its
# index -- exactly as the braced twin merges.
# A NUMERIC key is a KEY OF THE ELEMENT MAP, never an index into the
# writes, no gap-filling nulls, nothing for a JavaScript array's shape
# to leak through (the divergence issue #40 recorded). A pair "aimed
# at" an occupied index is not aimed at anything: it is its own
# element, the neighbours untouched in both directions -- and an index
# PAST the end grows the list by one MAP, not by a hole.
# The map-level optional key is untouched and must stay that way.
# REQUIRED WINS (ADR-044, #298): a key is optional in a meet only where
# every side that declares it says so, and a side that does not declare
# it does not vote. Two statements merge by the same rule.
# The statements of one map, and the keys an include brings, vote the
# same way: a plain pair is a required vote, an include votes by its
# own optional list, and the directive itself is not a key.
